My job requires me to be flexible and to travel frequently, which is why I rely on public transit and taxis to get where I need to be.

Living with multiple chemical sensitivity means I’m very careful about the environments I enter. I avoid places with strong fumes, harsh cleaning products, or any chemicals that could trigger an allergic reaction. That sensitivity also makes it harder to work in traditional office settings, so the freelance nature of my work is a blessing. I can choose the venues that are safe and comfortable for me.

I’m not married, and I don’t have children. I’m proud of my independence and the way I’ve adapted to my circumstances. Even though I’m 64 and still working, I feel young at heart. I’ve learned that staying active, staying connected, and staying true to my own needs is the best way to keep going.

My condition does limit my daily travel in subtle ways—I have to plan routes that allow me to pause for a quick check, and I’m careful about the timing of my meals and medication. Still, I manage it well enough to keep up with my coursework and part‑time job.

I’m proud to be a homeowner at 21, a student, and a part‑time caregiver. My life is a balancing act of school, work, health, and family, but I keep moving forward—whether that’s riding the bus to the community college, driving as a passenger to a client’s home, or staying at home to prepare for the next day.

My job doesn’t have a fixed workplace—I travel to different campuses and sometimes work from home, but I still spend five days a week on the job, clocking about fifty hours each week.

I’m mentally and emotionally disabled, which sometimes makes the day‑to‑day grind a bit more challenging, but I’ve learned to manage it with therapy and a supportive network. I don’t have any visual or hearing impairments, and I don’t use a cane, walker, or wheelchair. I have a driver’s license, but I rely almost exclusively on public transit to get to work. I take the train—specifically the CTA, METRA, or NICTD lines—at least five times a week. I don’t have any daily travel limits; I’m able to get where I need to go without restrictions. My commute is a steady rhythm that keeps me connected to my students and my community.

I’m not Hispanic or Latino, and I don’t volunteer regularly, but I find fulfillment in teaching and in the sense of purpose it brings. The combination of my education, my role in technology, and my ability to navigate the public transit system lets me maintain a stable life while managing my mental and emotional health.
